title: E35 - Are Legal AI Assistants Moving In-House? GC AI Founder Cecilia Ziniti
author: Cecilia Ziniti

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Ziniti does not directly dispute Harvey’s prestige-led traction or infrastructure ambitions, but redirects the strategic emphasis from elite law firms to underserved in-house legal departments. She argues that corporate teams require broader support across regulatory, privacy, AI and international work, not merely law-firm or contract-centred workflows.
qs: Exactly, and I think it leaves a gap to where, there's other players in legal AI, Harvey, Legora, who focused tremendously on law firms.
And we have a really wide swath of departments for which contracts are a slice and an important slice, but certainly not the bulk of the legal work.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source documents rapid, broadening legal-AI uptake among in-house lawyers, based on classroom observations and platform customers, but does not address access to justice, meaningful legal help, service transformation, or whether adoption can close justice gaps.
qs: Now that number is down to 10% and more than I think 75% of people are using it daily or even hourly.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: Ziniti materially develops the cluster’s proposition by articulating two plausible routes: integration with existing CLM systems and direct AI use over document stores. Her acknowledgment that CLM retains workflow value reinforces the synthesis’s distinction between disruption of incumbent products and continued need for contract infrastructure.
qs: And I do think there will be a generation of companies, excuse me, there will be a generation of companies that skips CLM and goes straight to AI pointed at a doc store.

That being said, you know, CLM has a purpose, and there's people happy with the things that it does around kind of reminders of, you know, signature, approvals, kind of the, like, sort of idea to contract.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Ziniti accepts the central proposition that in-house legal AI must address business-facing work beyond contract storage or review. She materially develops it by identifying underserved regulatory, privacy and international workflows, and by making integration with the business systems where clients work a practical design requirement. Her CLM-displacement and privilege claims remain predictions rather than established results.
qs: And we have a really wide swath of departments for which contracts are a slice and an important slice, but certainly not the bulk of the legal work.
And so basically, like, we need to play nice with all of them.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: Ziniti accepts that AI strengthens in-house departments as buyers and enables selective substitution for outside legal services. She materially develops the proposition by arguing that distinct in-house incentives and recurring, company-specific workflows justify dedicated products, while retaining human verification and acknowledging coexistence with CLM rather than claiming universal replacement.
qs: Of course, we can talk about the billable hour, but the core idea is that if you're applying legal AI to the actual legal work, to do the analysis, to do the extraction, the summary, the comparison, to get creative about legal arguments that you're making, you are reducing, in point of fact, the legal services being provided.
But in general, I would say something that is an asset for us is people recognize, okay, the workflows are different.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Ziniti accepts the cluster’s core view that AI changes legal-service production and reallocates work rather than eliminating lawyers. She materially extends it by explaining why in-house departments are especially likely to drive that shift: they optimise for business outcomes, possess deeper company context and use AI through workflows distinct from law firms. Her support is primarily experiential and anecdotal rather than independent market-wide evidence.
qs: Of course, we can talk about the billable hour, but the core idea is that if you're applying legal AI to the actual legal work, to do the analysis, to do the extraction, the summary, the comparison, to get creative about legal arguments that you're making, you are reducing, in point of fact, the legal services being provided.
Of course, a corporate attorney retained by the company is going to know that company more deeply and use AI differently than someone supporting it, the same proxy statement across many things.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Ziniti accepts the cluster’s core augmentation thesis and materially extends it for in-house legal departments: trained lawyers remain central, while value depends on company-specific workflows, user education and integration with CLM and broader business systems. Her customer examples illustrate task-level gains and workflow redesign, although they are vendor-reported rather than comparative evidence and she gives limited attention to verification.
qs: But I would say like developers and lawyers were very discerning, were professionals, were made better with AI.
And so basically, like, we need to play nice with all of them.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Ziniti supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI creates value by amplifying trained professionals rather than replacing their expertise. Her customer and engineering anecdotes also align with task-level acceleration while retaining production obligations, but she does not materially develop the cluster’s claims about agentic workflow design, tacit-knowledge transfer, evaluation or human verification.
qs: But I would say like developers and lawyers were very discerning, were professionals, were made better with AI.
And having the training, having learned to lawyer and be a legal team pre-AI, gives you the opportunity to be better.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Ziniti supports the cluster’s core view that effective legal-AI use depends on expertise developed through prior legal training, and she reinforces the need for deliberate user education. Her account is more optimistic about automation freeing lawyers for complex work and does not directly establish that AI is eroding the associate apprenticeship pipeline.
qs: And having the training, having learned to lawyer and be a legal team pre-AI, gives you the opportunity to be better.
We also at this point have taught, I think we lifted up, like 7,500 lawyers have been through our classes.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Ziniti aligns with the cluster’s conditional optimism by advocating legal-AI skills and platform-independent prompting education. Her reasoning is experience-based and promotional rather than measured proof of adoption, productivity or transformation, consistent with the cluster’s distinction between enthusiasm and evidence.
qs: And so I would say, super bullish, super optimistic, and in particular, coming that my co-founder and I come from developer tools has been this amazing ability to see what's next.
Even if you go with another platform, that's 100% fine.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Ziniti supports the cluster’s buyer-side account: in-house teams pursue business outcomes rather than preserving law-firm revenue, and company-specific knowledge leads them to use AI through distinct workflows. Her claim that AI reduces units of legal service also reinforces pressure on provider economics, though she does not address verification or the apprenticeship problem.
qs: That is not my goal as a general counsel, is to preserve the law firm revenue.
Of course, a corporate attorney retained by the company is going to know that company more deeply and use AI differently than someone supporting it, the same proxy statement across many things.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Ziniti directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: LLMs broaden legal software’s reach, but specialist value depends on legal workflows, citations and human verification. Her emphasis on in-house adoption and experiential training also aligns with the cluster’s view that workflow fit and organisational implementation matter, though her evidence is largely anecdotal rather than comparative.
qs: And then the third thing was basically just really workflows and initially prompts and now workflows around the things that lawyers in-house do.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Ziniti supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI adoption depends on guided learning and frontline experience rather than software provision alone. Her account adds an anecdote of user-led demand and a reinforcing cycle of use-case discovery, but does not provide measured evidence or materially extend the cluster’s organisational-change framework.
qs: That's like a part of your offering, not just the software itself.
Helping people experience that kicks off this virtuous cycle where then they're using it more, they're thinking of use cases.

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that in-house legal departments constitute an independent and potentially major market for legal AI, with adoption sometimes matching or exceeding law firms and demand spanning general-purpose, cross-market and in-house-specific products. Its evidence is observational and anecdotal, however, and does not establish adoption rates, durable vendor value or market concentration.
qs: One of the most surprising things to me is that the adoption of AI tools in-house has actually maintained pace, and in some instances, actually exceeded that of law firms.
But in addition to the chat GPTs of the world, the Geminis, which a lot of lawyers in-house are using, there are products that are specifically targeting in-house legal.

kp.k: In-house AI adoption challenges law-firm-led diffusion
kp.d: Host Zach Abramowitz frames in-house AI adoption as keeping pace with, and sometimes exceeding, law firms, contrary to his expectation that firms would lead investment and guide clients. He identifies products specifically targeting corporate legal teams as an important 2026 trend, alongside general-purpose AI and vendors serving both firms and departments; this is his observation rather than a comparative study presented in the episode.
qs: One of the most surprising things to me is that the adoption of AI tools in-house has actually maintained pace, and in some instances, actually exceeded that of law firms.
And I think this is one of the most important trends to watch in 2026.

kp.k: Specialised legal AI combines precision, citations and workflows
kp.d: GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti attributes the product's origin to seeing agentic software-engineering capabilities as transferable to legal work. She says LLMs made AI adequate for legal tasks and describes investment in answer accuracy, citations enabling lawyers to check work, and in-house-specific prompts and workflows. She reports serving a thousand companies worldwide, without presenting independent product-performance evidence.
qs: AI was never good enough for legal work until LLMS.
And then realized, okay, lawyers need citations too. We got to check our work.
And then the third thing was basically just really workflows and initially prompts and now workflows around the things that lawyers in-house do.
So right now we work with a thousand companies, in-house lawyers from all over the world.

kp.k: Education helps turn experimentation into sustained adoption
kp.d: Ziniti argues that experiencing an immediate improvement in legal work encourages further use and discovery of applications. She positions training as user empowerment and a means of accelerating departmental transformation, reporting that approximately 7,500 lawyers have attended the company's classes. Abramowitz likewise recommends avoiding barriers that delay users experiencing AI's capabilities.
qs: Helping people experience that kicks off this virtuous cycle where then they're using it more, they're thinking of use cases.
We also at this point have taught, I think we lifted up, like 7,500 lawyers have been through our classes.
And I tell legal teams, like, don't put a lot of barriers between your people, seeing what it is they can accomplish with AI.

kp.k: AI complements CLM while potentially bypassing it
kp.d: Ziniti says GC AI is not a contract lifecycle management system and must work with existing legal and business software. She recounts a customer using GC AI for migration extraction after its CLM provider could not do the work or would charge 60 grand in professional services. APIs and CLM integration are development priorities. She explicitly labels as a bold prediction the possibility that some companies will skip CLM for AI applied to document stores, while acknowledging CLM's continuing role in reminders, signatures and approvals.
qs: We're not a CLM, and the rest of the business workflow is this kind of thing.
And their CLM provider said, okay, no, we can't do it or we're in charge of 60 grand professional services to do it.
CLM integration is one of our most requested features.
And I do think there will be a generation of companies, excuse me, there will be a generation of companies that skips CLM and goes straight to AI pointed at a doc store.

kp.k: In-house work extends substantially beyond contract review
kp.d: Both speakers reject treating corporate legal departments as predominantly contract-redlining operations. Ziniti describes demand for regulatory, privacy, FDA, product and international work that traditional legal software and law-firm-focused AI have underserved. She associates in-house growth with bringing legal work closer to business operations and offers an explicitly tentative growth comparison: '87% more year over year the last 25 years than law firms,' without supplying the underlying source or explaining that measure in the transcript.
qs: there's a whole swath of legal that exactly as you said, isn't served by traditional software.
it's grown, basically I think it was 87% more year over year the last 25 years than law firms.
So we have companies that are, we have medical device companies on the platform doing all kinds of FDA work.
And we have a really wide swath of departments for which contracts are a slice and an important slice, but certainly not the bulk of the legal work.

kp.k: Buyer incentives differ from law-firm revenue preservation
kp.d: Ziniti argues that AI-assisted analysis, extraction, summarisation and comparison reduce the legal services supplied under the law-firm model, whereas general counsel prioritise business outcomes rather than preserving outside-counsel revenue. She contrasts competitively rebid outside work at Amazon, recalling average discounts of roughly 30% or 40%, with trusted, embedded internal counsel. This is her business-model argument and recollection, not a measured finding about AI's effect on firm revenue.
qs: you are reducing, in point of fact, the legal services being provided.
That is not my goal as a general counsel, is to preserve the law firm revenue. I want to win. I want to get the product launched.
If I recall correctly, the average discount that Amazon would get was something like 30% or 40%, some like huge number.
Embedded in the business, part of the business itself.

kp.k: In-house specialisation differentiates competing legal AI vendors
kp.d: Ziniti says GC AI competes with Harvey and Legora relatively frequently for corporate legal customers and does not always win. She argues that serving both firms and their buyers creates an inherent commercial tension for competitors, while repeated review of the same contract and company-specific proxy-season support require distinctive workflows and deep business familiarity. She acknowledges competitors' product strengths rather than claiming universal superiority.
qs: Who is the one who retains outside council? Of course, it's in-house.
but they're inherently always going to have this tension, right? Of who's making their money.
And, you know, we don't win every time. I welcome the competition.
Like reviewing the same contract many times. That's not something that law firms typically do, right?

kp.k: General-purpose AI sets the competitive floor
kp.d: Ziniti identifies foundation models as GC AI's largest competitive challenge. She claims differentiation through precise, cited legal answers and customised workflows rather than generic responses, illustrating this with detailed termination provisions and a customer's contract-risk memo that previously took two hours. The company tracks text copied out as an indicator of user value; the episode gives no comparative benchmark or quantified post-adoption time for that memo.
qs: It means that our product has to clear that floor.
The real answer is that it terminates for material breach on 60 days notice with a cure period per section 8.2.
We track a metric, which is what do people copy out of the platform?
It used to be a two-hour process, basically of like summarizing it, doing this and that.
But you're absolutely right that our biggest competition is the foundation models.

kp.k: Privilege protection remains an asserted, untested differentiator
kp.d: Ziniti presents confidentiality and privilege as major purchasing considerations, arguing that an isolated, secure tool sold only to legal teams would have a stronger privilege position than generalist AI. She reports Sam Altman's discouragement of treating ChatGPT as privileged and expressly says the issue has not yet been litigated. Her argument is therefore a vendor's prospective legal position, not a court finding or established privilege guarantee.
qs: We only sell to legal teams. It's isolated. We have all that security.
This issue has not yet to be litigated, because we watch.
That we have a really great case on privilege in a way that the generalist models do not.
And then, of course, a huge consideration is the confidentiality and the privilege issues.

kp.k: Class polling suggests sharply increased legal AI use
kp.d: Ziniti reports that when she began asking class participants about AI use for legal work, approximately two years earlier, more than 50% said never; that response is now down to 10%, while she estimates more than 75% use it daily or hourly. These are observations from her classes, with no respondent count or sampling methodology supplied. She also reports four banks, insurers and a newly signed large cement manufacturer's legal team on the platform as evidence that adoption extends beyond technology companies.
qs: So this is going on two years ago. And at the time, more than 50% of people would say never. Now that number is down to 10% and more than I think 75% of people are using it daily or even hourly.
we've got four banks on the platform, we've got insurance companies, we just signed a very large cement manufacturers legal team.
So this is not just a tech phenomenon.

kp.d: Ziniti argues that experienced lawyers and legal team members are well suited to prompting and directing AI, with in-house lawyers additionally accustomed to adapting to their clients' technologies. Her developer-tools analogy presents lawyers as professionals made more capable by AI, including when clients themselves experiment with 'vibe lawyering.' She treats pre-AI professional training as an advantage, rather than proposing that AI makes legal expertise unnecessary.
qs: the fact that you are an experienced lawyer or legal team member is a good thing because you're probably good at prompting and directing the AI.
you kind of have to meet the clients where they are, which means a certain amount of willingness and readiness to do new things.
But I would say like developers and lawyers were very discerning, were professionals, were made better with AI.
And having the training, having learned to lawyer and be a legal team pre-AI, gives you the opportunity to be better.

kp.k: Customer anecdote illustrates work retained in-house
kp.d: Ziniti describes a customer needing employee-app terms of use by the following day. The team had intended to call outside counsel, who could not meet the need, but instead adapted existing documents and compared other employee-app terms using the platform. She characterises the result as high quality. This illustrates her claim that AI can expand internal delivery capacity and avoid an outside instruction in an individual matter, without establishing a broader spending or quality effect.
qs: we've got to launch a new terms of use for an employee app that we're launching, timeline is tomorrow.
And they were originally going to call council on it. But council couldn't even do it.
They get it done by adapting their consumer terms of use and then something else that they had.
And they get it done at a very high level of quality benchmarking for other employee app terms of use in the process using the platform.

kp.k: Developer productivity provides an analogy for legal transformation
kp.d: Ziniti reports that GC AI supported many millions in revenue with just four engineers for a long period, attributing this capacity to AI augmentation. She recounts her co-founder largely building a settings page on a plane that otherwise would have taken a week, while noting that security and production work still had to be completed. She uses this internal software-development experience to inform expectations and product design for legal work, rather than presenting it as measured legal productivity evidence.
qs: for a long while, we had just four engineers and we're supporting many millions of revenue.
My co-founder basically mostly did it on the plane.
Obviously, we've got security, production stuff we've got to do, which we did.
But something like that would have taken a week otherwise.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cecilia Ziniti presents legal AI as an increasingly mainstream tool that augments in-house lawyers, changes legal workflows and purchasing incentives, and may substitute for some traditional software and externally purchased work.
pts.d: Ziniti claims that LLMs made AI suitable for legal work and that lawyer-specific accuracy improvements, citations and workflows make specialist products more useful than general-purpose models. She says experienced lawyers can become more capable and do more interesting work with AI, drawing an analogy with AI-assisted software developers rather than predicting wholesale lawyer replacement. She reports rapid adoption extending beyond technology companies and argues that practical education accelerates use. She characterises legal AI as a new software category that currently complements CLM but can perform tasks that CLM does not deliver satisfactorily; she explicitly predicts that some future companies will skip CLM and use AI over a document store. She identifies regulatory, privacy, product and international work as underserved opportunities beyond contract review. She argues that AI applied to analysis, extraction, summaries, comparisons and legal arguments reduces the legal services being provided by firms, creating tension between protecting firm revenue and in-house buyers' business objectives. An employee-app terms-of-use example illustrates work completed internally that the customer had intended to refer to outside counsel. She claims GC AI's legal results remain superior to general-purpose alternatives and identifies foundation models as its biggest competition, while acknowledging that it does not always beat Harvey or Legora. She also argues that a private, lawyer-specific tool has a stronger potential privilege argument than a generalist tool, expressly presenting this as an unlitigated position rather than an established legal outcome. Her roadmap includes potential law-firm partnerships and an eventual outside-counsel portal.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of Ziniti's professional experience, self-reported customer and training figures, informal participant polling, product-use metrics and customer anecdotes.
pts.d: Ziniti grounds her account in ten years as a general counsel, almost twenty years as a lawyer, early LLM access in 2022 and experience with developer tools. She reports serving a thousand companies and teaching approximately 7,500 lawyers. For adoption, she compares answers to a question asked in her classes: more than 50% initially said they never used AI for legal work, versus 10% at the time of the interview, while approximately 75% now reportedly use it daily or hourly. The transcript does not specify sample sizes, comparable respondent cohorts or survey methodology; these are figures about her class participants, not an identified representative profession-wide survey. Banks, insurers and a cement manufacturer's legal team provide examples of adoption outside technology. Workflow evidence includes a customer using GC AI for extraction during a CLM migration after its provider reportedly could not do the work or proposed a $60,000 professional-services charge; a contract risk memo formerly requiring two hours; and an employee-app terms-of-use task completed against a next-day deadline using existing documents and comparison with other terms. No post-AI completion time is supplied for the risk memo. Claimed superiority over general-purpose tools is supported by an illustrative contract-termination answer, reported customer reactions and tracking what users copy from the platform, not a named comparative benchmark or measured hallucination rate. The prediction that companies will bypass CLM is labelled a bold prediction. The privilege proposition is Ziniti's prospective legal argument, not a reported adjudicated finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims describe experience up to the 2026 interview; adoption is compared over roughly two years, while CLM bypass and outside-counsel connectivity are prospective and conditional.
pts.d: Ziniti places her initial transformative LLM experience in spring 2022 and describes the adoption shift across approximately two years preceding the interview. Customer counts, product superiority and workflow examples are presented as current or already experienced. She conditions specialist AI's value on better legal results, precise citations, tailored workflows, confidentiality, integrations and users learning to direct the system. Citations support human checking of output; she does not frame them as eliminating verification. Her optimism particularly concerns professionals who already know how to practise law and can prompt and direct AI. She says GC AI is not currently a CLM, acknowledges that building wider business workflows takes time and recognises continuing CLM functions such as reminders, signatures and approvals. No date is given for companies bypassing CLM. Potential law-firm partnerships and experiments are expected to develop 'this year,' meaning 2026 in the episode's framing; the portal is described only as eventual. The privilege argument remains explicitly contingent on future litigation. She qualifies competitive claims by acknowledging that GC AI does not win every contest and that competitors have product strengths.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate legal departments and their business clients, with consequences for outside law firms, legal-software vendors and general-purpose AI providers.
pts.d: In-house counsel and legal-team members are portrayed as gaining capacity, precision and the ability to support business goals across contracts, privacy, regulatory compliance, product launches and international matters. Ziniti argues that their existing need to adapt to their business clients' technology makes them particularly receptive to AI. Examples span technology businesses, banks, insurers, a cement manufacturer, medical-device companies doing FDA work and consumer companies handling privacy matters. The corporate client benefits described are improved business support and faster internal delivery, not individual access to justice. Outside law firms face buyers whose goals are not to preserve firm revenue and who may perform some previously external work themselves. Vendors serving both firms and departments face what Ziniti describes as conflicting customer incentives and distinct workflows. Harvey and Legora are discussed as competing software providers, not alternative legal service providers. CLM vendors face both integration demand and potential bypass by a future generation of customers; foundation-model providers compete directly with specialist legal AI. Ziniti's account emphasises augmentation of experienced professionals and does not supply a quantified prediction of job losses or staffing changes.
